But their eyes were holden that they should not know him. And he said unto them, What manner of communications are these that ye have one to another, as ye walk, and are sad? And the one of them, whose name was Cleopas, answering said unto him, Art thou only a stranger in Jerusalem, and hast not known the things which are come to pass there in these days? And he said unto them, What things? And they said unto him, Concerning Jesus of Nazareth, which was a prophet mighty in deed and word before God and all the people: and how the chief priests and our rulers delivered him to be condemned to death, and have crucified him. But we trusted that it had been he which should have redeemed Israel: and beside all this, to day is the third day since these things were done. Yea, and certain women also of our company made us astonished, which were early at the sepulchre; and when they found not his body, they came, saying, that they had also seen a vision of angels, which said that he was alive. And certain of them which were with us went to the sepulchre, and found it even so as the women had said: but him they saw not. Then he said unto them, O fools, and slow of heart to believe all that the prophets have spoken: ought not Christ to have suffered these things, and to enter into his glory? And beginning at Moses and all the prophets, he expounded unto them in all the scriptures the things concerning himself. And they drew nigh unto the village, whither they went: and he made as though he would have gone further. But they constrained him, saying, Abide with us: for it is toward evening, and the day is far spent. And he went in to tarry with them. And it came to pass, as he sat at meat with them, he took bread, and blessed it, and brake, and gave to them. And their eyes were opened, and they knew him; and he vanished out of their sight. And they said one to another, Did not our heart burn within us, while he talked with us by the way, and while he opened to us the scriptures? And they rose up the same hour, and returned to Jerusalem, and found the eleven gathered together, and them that were with them, saying, The Lord is risen indeed, and hath appeared to Simon. And they told what things were done in the way, and how he was known of them in breaking of bread.
studies.context: Two disciples walk away from Jerusalem, crushed, telling a "stranger" how their hopes died. He opens the Scriptures until their hearts burn — yet they recognize him only when he breaks the bread at table, and then he vanishes.
studies.orthodox: The Church reads Emmaus as the shape of her worship: the risen Christ is met in the Scriptures opened and the bread broken (St. Luke structures it like a liturgy). Recognition comes at the table, and the walk back to Jerusalem replaces the walk away.
studies.practice: Read one Old Testament passage today looking for Christ in it, the way he taught on the road. Then share one meal with thanksgiving said out loud.
questions: Why do the disciples not recognize Jesus on the road, though their hearts burn?
They were walking away from Jerusalem. Where do you walk when disappointed with God?

quiz.prompt: When do the disciples finally recognize him?
choices: In the breaking of the bread
When he shows them his hands
quiz.explanation: Luke 24:30–31: known in the breaking of the bread — eyes opened at the table.

quiz.prompt: What do they say about the road afterward?
choices: "Our hearts burned within us while he opened the Scriptures"
"We knew him from the first mile"
quiz.explanation: Luke 24:32: hearts burned under the opened Scriptures before eyes were opened at the table.

studies.title: Teach us to pray
studies.passage: And when thou prayest, thou shalt not be as the hypocrites are: for they love to pray standing in the synagogues and in the corners of the streets, that they may be seen of men. Verily I say unto you, They have their reward. But thou, when thou prayest, enter into thy closet, and when thou hast shut thy door, pray to thy Father which is in secret; and thy Father which seeth in secret shall reward thee openly. But when ye pray, use not vain repetitions, as the heathen do: for they think that they shall be heard for their much speaking. Be not ye therefore like unto them: for your Father knoweth what things ye have need of, before ye ask him. After this manner therefore pray ye: Our Father which art in heaven, Hallowed be thy name. Thy kingdom come. Thy will be done in earth, as it is in heaven. Give us this day our daily bread. And forgive us our debts, as we forgive our debtors. And lead us not into temptation, but deliver us from evil: For thine is the kingdom, and the power, and the glory, for ever. Amen. For if ye forgive men their trespasses, your heavenly Father will also forgive you: but if ye forgive not men their trespasses, neither will your Father forgive your trespasses.
studies.context: Jesus warns against praying to be seen and against babbling, then gives the pattern prayer: Father, kingdom, daily bread, forgiveness tied to our forgiving, and deliverance from evil.
studies.orthodox: The Church has prayed these exact words at every liturgy for two thousand years (St. Cyprian calls it the summary of the gospel). "Our Father" — never "my Father" alone: even private prayer is prayed as a member of a family.
studies.practice: Pray the Lord's Prayer once today at half your normal speed. Camp on the line that costs you most and stay there a while.
questions: Why does the prayer begin with God's name and kingdom before our needs?
"Forgive us our debts, as we forgive" — what is Jesus doing by chaining those two together?

quiz.prompt: How does Jesus say not to pray?
choices: To be seen by others, with empty repetition
quiz.explanation: Matthew 6:5–7: the prayer is against performance and babble, not against written words.

quiz.prompt: What bread does the prayer ask for?
choices: Bread enough to store for the year
quiz.explanation: Matthew 6:11: daily bread trains daily dependence.

studies.title: Tongues of fire
studies.passage: And when the day of Pentecost was fully come, they were all with one accord in one place. And suddenly there came a sound from heaven as of a rushing mighty wind, and it filled all the house where they were sitting. And there appeared unto them cloven tongues like as of fire, and it sat upon each of them. And they were all filled with the Holy Ghost, and began to speak with other tongues, as the Spirit gave them utterance. And there were dwelling at Jerusalem Jews, devout men, out of every nation under heaven. Now when this was noised abroad, the multitude came together, and were confounded, because that every man heard them speak in his own language. And they were all amazed and marvelled, saying one to another, Behold, are not all these which speak Galilæans? And how hear we every man in our own tongue, wherein we were born? Parthians, and Medes, and Elamites, and the dwellers in Mesopotamia, and in Judæa, and Cappadocia, in Pontus, and Asia, Phrygia, and Pamphylia, in Egypt, and in the parts of Libya about Cyrene, and strangers of Rome, Jews and proselytes, Cretes and Arabians, we do hear them speak in our tongues the wonderful works of God. And they were all amazed, and were in doubt, saying one to another, What meaneth this? Others mocking said, These men are full of new wine. … Therefore let all the house of Israel know assuredly, that God hath made that same Jesus, whom ye have crucified, both Lord and Christ. Now when they heard this, they were pricked in their heart, and said unto Peter and to the rest of the apostles, Men and brethren, what shall we do? Then Peter said unto them, Repent, and be baptized every one of you in the name of Jesus Christ for the remission of sins, and ye shall receive the gift of the Holy Ghost. For the promise is unto you, and to your children, and to all that are afar off, even as many as the Lord our God shall call. And with many other words did he testify and exhort, saying, Save yourselves from this untoward generation. Then they that gladly received his word were baptized: and the same day there were added unto them about three thousand souls.
studies.context: Fifty days after Passover, wind and fire fill the house; the apostles speak and every nation hears in its own language. Peter preaches the crucified and risen Christ; three thousand are baptized that day.
studies.orthodox: Pentecost reverses Babel: languages divide in pride, the Spirit unites in confession without erasing the nations — each hears in his own tongue. The Church is born preaching, not waiting to feel ready.
studies.practice: Pray for one person by name to receive courage today, and if the moment comes, say one plain sentence about Christ without arguing.
questions: At Babel tongues scatter; at Pentecost tongues gather. What makes the difference?
The crowd is cut to the heart and asks, "What shall we do?" What does Peter answer first?

quiz.prompt: What visibly rests on each apostle?
quiz.explanation: Acts 2:3: cloven tongues like as of fire sat upon each of them.

quiz.prompt: How many are baptized that day?
quiz.explanation: Acts 2:41: about three thousand souls added that day.

studies.title: Lord, lay not this sin to their charge
studies.passage: When they heard these things, they were cut to the heart, and they gnashed on him with their teeth. But he, being full of the Holy Ghost, looked up stedfastly into heaven, and saw the glory of God, and Jesus standing on the right hand of God, and said, Behold, I see the heavens opened, and the Son of man standing on the right hand of God. Then they cried out with a loud voice, and stopped their ears, and ran upon him with one accord, and cast him out of the city, and stoned him: and the witnesses laid down their clothes at a young man's feet, whose name was Saul. And they stoned Stephen, calling upon God, and saying, Lord Jesus, receive my spirit. And he kneeled down, and cried with a loud voice, Lord, lay not this sin to their charge. And when he had said this, he fell asleep. … And Saul was consenting unto his death. And at that time there was a great persecution against the church which was at Jerusalem; and they were all scattered abroad throughout the regions of Judæa and Samaria, except the apostles.
studies.context: Stephen, full of the Spirit, sees heaven opened and the Son of Man standing at God's right hand. As stones crush him, he prays twice: receive my spirit — and forgive them. A young man named Saul holds the coats.
studies.orthodox: Stephen is the Church's first martyr, and his death copies his Master's word for word (Luke 23:34, 46). St. Augustine said the Church owes Paul's conversion to Stephen's prayer: the man holding the coats became the apostle.
studies.practice: Pray today for one person who has wronged you — by name, asking God genuinely not to hold it against them.
questions: Why does Stephen see the Son of Man standing, when Daniel and the creed picture him seated?
What might your forgiveness-prayer set in motion that you will never see?

quiz.prompt: What does Stephen see before his death?
choices: An angel coming to rescue him
Heaven opened, and the Son of Man standing at the right hand of God
quiz.explanation: Acts 7:55–56: the only place the risen Christ is seen standing — as if rising for his witness.

quiz.prompt: What is Stephen's last prayer?
choices: "Lord, lay not this sin to their charge"
quiz.explanation: Acts 7:60: dying, he intercedes for his killers.

studies.title: Saul, Saul, why persecutest thou me?
studies.passage: And Saul, yet breathing out threatenings and slaughter against the disciples of the Lord, went unto the high priest, and desired of him letters to Damascus to the synagogues, that if he found any of this way, whether they were men or women, he might bring them bound unto Jerusalem. And as he journeyed, he came near Damascus: and suddenly there shined round about him a light from heaven: and he fell to the earth, and heard a voice saying unto him, Saul, Saul, why persecutest thou me? And he said, Who art thou, Lord? And the Lord said, I am Jesus whom thou persecutest: it is hard for thee to kick against the pricks. And he trembling and astonished said, Lord, what wilt thou have me to do? And the Lord said unto him, Arise, and go into the city, and it shall be told thee what thou must do. And the men which journeyed with him stood speechless, hearing a voice, but seeing no man. And Saul arose from the earth; and when his eyes were opened, he saw no man: but they led him by the hand, and brought him into Damascus. And he was three days without sight, and neither did eat nor drink. And there was a certain disciple at Damascus, named Ananias; and to him said the Lord in a vision, Ananias. And he said, Behold, I am here, Lord. And the Lord said unto him, Arise, and go into the street which is called Straight, and enquire in the house of Judas for one called Saul, of Tarsus: for, behold, he prayeth, and hath seen in a vision a man named Ananias coming in, and putting his hand on him, that he might receive his sight. Then Ananias answered, Lord, I have heard by many of this man, how much evil he hath done to thy saints at Jerusalem: and here he hath authority from the chief priests to bind all that call on thy name. But the Lord said unto him, Go thy way: for he is a chosen vessel unto me, to bear my name before the Gentiles, and kings, and the children of Israel: for I will shew him how great things he must suffer for my name's sake. And Ananias went his way, and entered into the house; and putting his hands on him said, Brother Saul, the Lord, even Jesus, that appeared unto thee in the way as thou camest, hath sent me, that thou mightest receive thy sight, and be filled with the Holy Ghost. And immediately there fell from his eyes as it had been scales: and he received sight forthwith, and arose, and was baptized. And when he had received meat, he was strengthened. Then was Saul certain days with the disciples which were at Damascus.
studies.context: Breathing threats, Saul rides to arrest Christians and meets the risen Christ in blinding light: "I am Jesus whom thou persecutest." Blind, he is led by the hand; a frightened disciple, Ananias, baptizes him, and the persecutor becomes the apostle.
studies.orthodox: The Church notes the details: Christ identifies himself with his suffering people ("thou persecutest me"), and he sends Saul not a private vision to keep but to the Church — to be baptized, filled, and taught. Conversion is personal and ecclesial at once.
studies.practice: Name one area where you may be "kicking against the goads." Surrender it today in prayer, then tell one Christian friend.
questions: Why does Jesus say "thou persecutest me" when Saul was arresting ordinary believers?
God could have taught Saul directly. Why send Ananias and baptism instead?

quiz.prompt: What is Saul doing when stopped?
choices: Traveling to Damascus to arrest Christians
quiz.explanation: Acts 9:1–3: mid-persecution, letters in hand, he meets Christ.

quiz.prompt: What restores Saul's sight?
choices: Ananias lays hands on him; scales fall; he is baptized
The light slowly fading over three weeks
quiz.explanation: Acts 9:17–18: healing and baptism come through the Church he was attacking.

studies.title: It seemed good to the Holy Spirit and to us
studies.passage: And the apostles and elders came together for to consider of this matter. And when there had been much disputing, Peter rose up, and said unto them, Men and brethren, ye know how that a good while ago God made choice among us, that the Gentiles by my mouth should hear the word of the gospel, and believe. And God, which knoweth the hearts, bare them witness, giving them the Holy Ghost, even as he did unto us; and put no difference between us and them, purifying their hearts by faith. Now therefore why tempt ye God, to put a yoke upon the neck of the disciples, which neither our fathers nor we were able to bear? But we believe that through the grace of the Lord Jesus Christ we shall be saved, even as they. Then all the multitude kept silence, and gave audience to Barnabas and Paul, declaring what miracles and wonders God had wrought among the Gentiles by them. And after they had held their peace, James answered, saying, Men and brethren, hearken unto me: Simeon hath declared how God at the first did visit the Gentiles, to take out of them a people for his name. And to this agree the words of the prophets; as it is written, After this I will return, And will build again the tabernacle of David, which is fallen down; And I will build again the ruins thereof, And I will set it up: That the residue of men might seek after the Lord, And all the Gentiles, upon whom my name is called, Saith the Lord, who doeth all these things. Known unto God are all his works from the beginning of the world. Wherefore my sentence is, that we trouble not them, which from among the Gentiles are turned to God: but that we write unto them, that they abstain from pollutions of idols, and from fornication, and from things strangled, and from blood. For Moses of old time hath in every city them that preach him, being read in the synagogues every sabbath day. … For it seemed good to the Holy Ghost, and to us, to lay upon you no greater burden than these necessary things; that ye abstain from meats offered to idols, and from blood, and from things strangled, and from fornication: from which if ye keep yourselves, ye shall do well. Fare ye well.
studies.context: Must Gentile believers be circumcised and keep the law of Moses to be saved? The apostles and elders gather in Jerusalem, hear testimony, search Scripture, and write one letter: the Spirit and the Church deciding together, giving no greater burden than necessary.
studies.orthodox: Acts 15 is the Church's first council and her pattern ever since: bishops and presbyters, Scripture and lived witness, decision by consensus under the Spirit. The faith is kept by gathering, not by each teacher deciding alone.
studies.practice: When you hit a hard question of faith, do what the Church did: bring it to Scripture and to the Church rather than deciding solo. Ask one mature believer this week.
questions: Peter's testimony about Cornelius matters as much as James's Scripture. Why does the council need both?
The letter gives "no greater burden than necessary." What does pastoral restraint look like in giving advice?

quiz.prompt: What question forced the council?
choices: Whether to build a temple in Antioch
Whether Gentile converts must be circumcised and keep the law to be saved
Whether Paul should travel with Barnabas
quiz.explanation: Acts 15:1, 5: salvation itself was the question on the table.

quiz.prompt: How does the letter describe its own authority?
choices: "It seemed good to the Holy Spirit, and to us"
quiz.explanation: Acts 15:28: the Spirit and the gathered Church speak in one sentence.

studies.title: Born of water and the Spirit
studies.passage: There was a man of the Pharisees, named Nicodemus, a ruler of the Jews: the same came to Jesus by night, and said unto him, Rabbi, we know that thou art a teacher come from God: for no man can do these miracles that thou doest, except God be with him. Jesus answered and said unto him, Verily, verily, I say unto thee, Except a man be born again, he cannot see the kingdom of God. Nicodemus saith unto him, How can a man be born when he is old? can he enter the second time into his mother's womb, and be born? Jesus answered, Verily, verily, I say unto thee, Except a man be born of water and of the Spirit, he cannot enter into the kingdom of God. That which is born of the flesh is flesh; and that which is born of the Spirit is spirit. Marvel not that I said unto thee, Ye must be born again. The wind bloweth where it listeth, and thou hearest the sound thereof, but canst not tell whence it cometh, and whither it goeth: so is every one that is born of the Spirit.
studies.context: Nicodemus comes by night and hears a hard saying: "Except a man be born again, he cannot see the kingdom of God." Jesus explains: born of water and of the Spirit — like wind, unseen in origin, real in effect.
studies.orthodox: The Church has read "water and the Spirit" as baptism from the earliest Fathers (St. Justin, St. Irenaeus): the new birth is not a feeling about God but God's own act, washing and giving the Spirit. Nicodemus, the teacher of Israel, must become a child again.
studies.practice: Thank God today for your baptism (or, if unbaptized, ask him plainly to bring you to the water). Pray for one person by name to be born anew.
questions: Why does a respected teacher need to be "born again" rather than simply learn more?
Jesus compares the Spirit to wind. What does that free us from trying to control?

quiz.prompt: What two things does Jesus name for the new birth?
quiz.explanation: John 3:5: "born of water and of the Spirit" — read by the early Church as baptism.

quiz.prompt: Why does Nicodemus struggle with the saying?
choices: He takes "born again" as a second physical birth
quiz.explanation: John 3:4: he hears birth as biology; Jesus speaks of a birth from above.

studies.title: This is my body
studies.passage: And as they were eating, Jesus took bread, and blessed it, and brake it, and gave it to the disciples, and said, Take, eat; this is my body. And he took the cup, and gave thanks, and gave it to them, saying, Drink ye all of it; for this is my blood of the new testament, which is shed for many for the remission of sins. But I say unto you, I will not drink henceforth of this fruit of the vine, until that day when I drink it new with you in my Father's kingdom. And when they had sung an hymn, they went out into the mount of Olives. … For I have received of the Lord that which also I delivered unto you, That the Lord Jesus the same night in which he was betrayed took bread: and when he had given thanks, he brake it, and said, Take, eat: this is my body, which is broken for you: this do in remembrance of me. After the same manner also he took the cup, when he had supped, saying, This cup is the new testament in my blood: this do ye, as oft as ye drink it, in remembrance of me. For as often as ye eat this bread, and drink this cup, ye do shew the Lord's death till he come. Wherefore whosoever shall eat this bread, and drink this cup of the Lord, unworthily, shall be guilty of the body and blood of the Lord. But let a man examine himself, and so let him eat of that bread, and drink of that cup. For he that eateth and drinketh unworthily, eateth and drinketh damnation to himself, not discerning the Lord's body.
studies.context: At the Last Supper Jesus takes bread, blesses, breaks, and gives: "Take, eat; this is my body." Paul, passing on what he received, warns the Corinthians to examine themselves and discern the body, so the meal heals rather than judges.
studies.orthodox: The Church takes the Lord at his word: the gifts are truly his Body and Blood, received in faith with preparation — fasting, repentance, reconciliation. Paul's warning means the meal is reality, not symbol only; realities can be received carelessly.
studies.practice: Before your next meal, practice small preparation: confess one sin quietly, forgive one person, then eat with thanksgiving. Bring that pattern toward the chalice.
questions: Why would Paul warn about eating "unworthily" if the supper were only a reminder picture?
What preparation does this passage itself name?

quiz.prompt: What does Jesus say over the bread?
choices: "This will become a symbol of me"
quiz.explanation: Matthew 26:26: the words are direct — "this is my body."

quiz.prompt: What does Paul instruct before eating?
quiz.explanation: 1 Corinthians 11:28: self-examination and discerning the body.

studies.title: My flesh is food indeed
studies.passage: I am that bread of life. Your fathers did eat manna in the wilderness, and are dead. This is the bread which cometh down from heaven, that a man may eat thereof, and not die. I am the living bread which came down from heaven: if any man eat of this bread, he shall live for ever: and the bread that I will give is my flesh, which I will give for the life of the world. The Jews therefore strove among themselves, saying, How can this man give us his flesh to eat? Then Jesus said unto them, Verily, verily, I say unto you, Except ye eat the flesh of the Son of man, and drink his blood, ye have no life in you. Whoso eateth my flesh, and drinketh my blood, hath eternal life; and I will raise him up at the last day. For my flesh is meat indeed, and my blood is drink indeed. He that eateth my flesh, and drinketh my blood, dwelleth in me, and I in him. As the living Father hath sent me, and I live by the Father: so he that eateth me, even he shall live by me. This is that bread which came down from heaven: not as your fathers did eat manna, and are dead: he that eateth of this bread shall live for ever.
studies.context: After feeding the five thousand, Jesus presses the sign: "Except ye eat the flesh of the Son of man, and drink his blood, ye have no life in you... For my flesh is meat indeed." Many disciples walk away; he lets them.
studies.orthodox: The Church notes Jesus does not soften the words when people stumble — he repeats them more strongly (the Greek even shifts to "chewing"). St. Ignatius of Antioch, within living memory of the apostles, calls the Eucharist "the medicine of immortality."
studies.practice: Read the passage once without trying to make it comfortable. Ask instead: what is Christ offering that I have been treating as optional?
questions: When hearers stumble, Jesus repeats the teaching more plainly instead of explaining it away. Why?
"Abide in me" (v.56) — what does eating have to do with abiding?

quiz.prompt: What does Jesus promise to the one who eats his flesh and drinks his blood?
choices: "I will raise him up at the last day"
quiz.explanation: John 6:54: eating is tied to resurrection, not only to present comfort.

quiz.prompt: How do many disciples respond?
choices: They walk back and follow him no more
They ask to see the Father
quiz.explanation: John 6:66: the hard saying empties the crowd — and Jesus does not chase them with a softer version.

studies.title: Hold the traditions
studies.passage: Therefore, brethren, stand fast, and hold the traditions which ye have been taught, whether by word, or our epistle. … But continue thou in the things which thou hast learned and hast been assured of, knowing of whom thou hast learned them; and that from a child thou hast known the holy scriptures, which are able to make thee wise unto salvation through faith which is in Christ Jesus. All scripture is given by inspiration of God, and is profitable for doctrine, for reproof, for correction, for instruction in righteousness: that the man of God may be perfect, throughly furnished unto all good works.
studies.context: Paul tells the Thessalonians to stand fast and hold the traditions taught "whether by word, or our epistle," and tells Timothy that Scripture, breathed by God, equips the man of God — the same Timothy who learned the faith at his grandmother's knee.
studies.orthodox: The Church reads these together: the apostolic faith comes by word and letter, one Tradition in two streams; Scripture is its God-breathed heart, never a do-it-yourself kit severed from the Church that received, kept, and canonized it.
studies.practice: Ask today: who handed the faith to me, and whose hands am I putting it into? Thank one of them, and teach one small thing to someone else.
questions: Paul names two channels — spoken word and letter. What happens to Christianity if one is thrown away?
Timothy knew the Scriptures from childhood — through family. What does that say about where the Bible is meant to be learned?

quiz.prompt: How were the traditions delivered, per Paul?
choices: By letter only, after his death
quiz.explanation: 2 Thessalonians 2:15: the spoken and written word are one apostolic teaching.

quiz.prompt: What is Scripture profitable for, in 2 Timothy 3?
choices: Doctrine, reproof, correction, instruction in righteousness
quiz.explanation: 2 Timothy 3:16–17: God-breathed Scripture equips the man of God for every good work.

studies.title: No condemnation, no separation
studies.passage: There is therefore now no condemnation to them which are in Christ Jesus, who walk not after the flesh, but after the Spirit. … For as many as are led by the Spirit of God, they are the sons of God. For ye have not received the spirit of bondage again to fear; but ye have received the Spirit of adoption, whereby we cry, Abba, Father. The Spirit itself beareth witness with our spirit, that we are the children of God: and if children, then heirs; heirs of God, and joint-heirs with Christ; if so be that we suffer with him, that we may be also glorified together. … And we know that all things work together for good to them that love God, to them who are the called according to his purpose. For whom he did foreknow, he also did predestinate to be conformed to the image of his Son, that he might be the firstborn among many brethren. Moreover whom he did predestinate, them he also called: and whom he called, them he also justified: and whom he justified, them he also glorified. What shall we then say to these things? If God be for us, who can be against us? He that spared not his own Son, but delivered him up for us all, how shall he not with him also freely give us all things? Who shall lay any thing to the charge of God's elect? It is God that justifieth. Who is he that condemneth? It is Christ that died, yea rather, that is risen again, who is even at the right hand of God, who also maketh intercession for us. Who shall separate us from the love of Christ? shall tribulation, or distress, or persecution, or famine, or nakedness, or peril, or sword? As it is written, For thy sake we are killed all the day long; We are accounted as sheep for the slaughter. Nay, in all these things we are more than conquerors through him that loved us. For I am persuaded, that neither death, nor life, nor angels, nor principalities, nor powers, nor things present, nor things to come, nor height, nor depth, nor any other creature, shall be able to separate us from the love of God, which is in Christ Jesus our Lord.
studies.context: Paul's summit: no condemnation for those in Christ; the Spirit makes slaves into sons who cry "Abba"; all things work together for good; and nothing — death, life, angels, powers — can separate us from the love of God in Christ.
studies.orthodox: The Fathers read Romans 8 as the Christian life itself: adoption, the Spirit's groaning prayer, and a love from which we cannot be separated — not a bare legal verdict but a family and a union. Suffering is named honestly and outweighed by glory (v.18).
studies.practice: Take the worst thing currently hanging over you and pray the end of this passage over it by name: "Nor [this] shall be able to separate me from the love of God."
questions: Paul says God works all things together for good "to them that love God" — how is that different from "everything happens for a reason"?
What does crying "Abba, Father" change that "obeying the rules" cannot?

quiz.prompt: What is there now for those in Christ Jesus?
quiz.explanation: Romans 8:1: "There is therefore now no condemnation."

quiz.prompt: What can separate us from the love of God?
quiz.explanation: Romans 8:38–39: Paul's list ends with "nor any other creature" — nothing.

studies.title: The greatest of these is love
studies.passage: Though I speak with the tongues of men and of angels, and have not charity, I am become as sounding brass, or a tinkling cymbal. And though I have the gift of prophecy, and understand all mysteries, and all knowledge; and though I have all faith, so that I could remove mountains, and have not charity, I am nothing. And though I bestow all my goods to feed the poor, and though I give my body to be burned, and have not charity, it profiteth me nothing. Charity suffereth long, and is kind; charity envieth not; charity vaunteth not itself, is not puffed up, doth not behave itself unseemly, seeketh not her own, is not easily provoked, thinketh no evil; rejoiceth not in iniquity, but rejoiceth in the truth; beareth all things, believeth all things, hopeth all things, endureth all things. Charity never faileth: but whether there be prophecies, they shall fail; whether there be tongues, they shall cease; whether there be knowledge, it shall vanish away. For we know in part, and we prophesy in part. But when that which is perfect is come, then that which is in part shall be done away. When I was a child, I spake as a child, I understood as a child, I thought as a child: but when I became a man, I put away childish things. For now we see through a glass, darkly; but then face to face: now I know in part; but then shall I know even as also I am known. And now abideth faith, hope, charity, these three; but the greatest of these is charity.
studies.context: Between chapters on spiritual gifts, Paul sets "a more excellent way": without love, tongues are noise, knowledge is nothing, even martyrdom profits nothing. Love is patient, does not keep score of wrongs, and never ends.
studies.orthodox: St. John Chrysostom calls this passage the portrait of Christ himself: read "love" as "Jesus" and every line lands. The Church measures gifts by love, not excitement; prophecy and knowledge pass, love remains into the age to come.
studies.practice: Choose the one line of this chapter you most fail at (envy? keeping records of wrongs?) and practice its opposite once today, concretely.
questions: Why would giving your body to be burned still profit nothing without love?
"Love does not keep a record of wrongs" (v.5) — whose record do you need to burn today?

quiz.prompt: Without love, what is a person with great gifts?
quiz.explanation: 1 Corinthians 13:1–3: gifts without love equal nothing, however spectacular.

quiz.prompt: What remains when prophecies and knowledge pass away?
choices: Faith, hope, and love — and the greatest is love
quiz.explanation: 1 Corinthians 13:13: love is greatest because love is eternal.

studies.title: The fruit of the Spirit
studies.passage: This I say then, Walk in the Spirit, and ye shall not fulfil the lust of the flesh. For the flesh lusteth against the Spirit, and the Spirit against the flesh: and these are contrary the one to the other: so that ye cannot do the things that ye would. But if ye be led of the Spirit, ye are not under the law. Now the works of the flesh are manifest, which are these; Adultery, fornication, uncleanness, lasciviousness, idolatry, witchcraft, hatred, variance, emulations, wrath, strife, seditions, heresies, envyings, murders, drunkenness, revellings, and such like: of the which I tell you before, as I have also told you in time past, that they which do such things shall not inherit the kingdom of God. But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, longsuffering, gentleness, goodness, faith, meekness, temperance: against such there is no law. And they that are Christ's have crucified the flesh with the affections and lusts. If we live in the Spirit, let us also walk in the Spirit.
studies.context: Paul sets flesh and Spirit at war, then shows the harvest of each. The Spirit's fruit is singular — one fruit with one flavor: love, joy, peace, longsuffering, gentleness, goodness, faith, meekness, temperance.
studies.orthodox: The Fathers read fruit, not fruits: the Spirit grows one integrated character the way a tree grows one kind of fruit. You do not manufacture fruit; you stay attached, crucify the flesh with its passions, and keep in step.
studies.practice: Pick one fruit-word and one flesh-work from the list. Feed the first and starve the second today, on purpose.
questions: Why does Paul say "fruit" (singular) but "works" (plural) of the flesh?
Which item on the fruit list is most missing in your home right now?

quiz.prompt: What are those who belong to Christ said to have done?
choices: Crucified the flesh with its affections and lusts
quiz.explanation: Galatians 5:24: crucifixion, not management, is the verb.

quiz.prompt: How are we told to walk?
choices: In the Spirit, keeping in step with the Spirit
quiz.explanation: Galatians 5:16, 25: walk in the Spirit and you will not fulfill the flesh.

studies.title: Put on the whole armor of God
studies.passage: Finally, my brethren, be strong in the Lord, and in the power of his might. Put on the whole armour of God, that ye may be able to stand against the wiles of the devil. For we wrestle not against flesh and blood, but against principalities, against powers, against the rulers of the darkness of this world, against spiritual wickedness in high places. Wherefore take unto you the whole armour of God, that ye may be able to withstand in the evil day, and having done all, to stand. Stand therefore, having your loins girt about with truth, and having on the breastplate of righteousness; and your feet shod with the preparation of the gospel of peace; above all, taking the shield of faith, wherewith ye shall be able to quench all the fiery darts of the wicked. And take the helmet of salvation, and the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God: praying always with all prayer and supplication in the Spirit, and watching thereunto with all perseverance and supplication for all saints;
studies.context: Paul tells a church in a pagan city that the real war is not against flesh and blood. Piece by piece he arms them — truth, righteousness, the gospel of peace, faith, salvation, the word of God — and finishes with praying at all times.
studies.orthodox: The Church reads the armor as Christ himself worn (Romans 13:14: "put ye on the Lord Jesus Christ"): truth is his belt before it is our honesty. Prayer is not the seventh piece; it is the air the soldier breathes.
studies.practice: Dress spiritually on purpose this morning: name each piece as you "put it on" in prayer before you leave the house.
questions: Why does Paul insist the enemy is not flesh and blood — what changes in how we fight people we disagree with?
The shield of faith quenches "fiery darts." What dart has been landing on you lately?

quiz.prompt: What is the sword of the Spirit?
quiz.explanation: Ephesians 6:17: the only offensive weapon listed is God's word.

quiz.prompt: What are we to do "at all times" as the armor is worn?
choices: Pray in the Spirit, watching with perseverance
Meet daily with the whole church
quiz.explanation: Ephesians 6:18: prayer at all times is the soldier's atmosphere.

studies.title: The peace that passes understanding
studies.passage: Rejoice in the Lord alway: and again I say, Rejoice. Let your moderation be known unto all men. The Lord is at hand. Be careful for nothing; but in every thing by prayer and supplication with thanksgiving let your requests be made known unto God. And the peace of God, which passeth all understanding, shall keep your hearts and minds through Christ Jesus. Finally, brethren, whatsoever things are true, whatsoever things are honest, whatsoever things are just, whatsoever things are pure, whatsoever things are lovely, whatsoever things are of good report; if there be any virtue, and if there be any praise, think on these things. Those things, which ye have both learned, and received, and heard, and seen in me, do: and the God of peace shall be with you.
studies.context: From prison Paul writes the Bible's recipe for anxiety: rejoice, be known for gentleness, refuse worry, pray with thanksgiving — and the peace of God will guard hearts and minds. Then: think on whatever is true, honest, just, pure, lovely.
studies.orthodox: The Church hears "guard" as a soldier's word: peace is a garrison posted over the heart, not a mood we manufacture. The prescription is not "feel better" but a sequence of acts — rejoice, pray, thank, think — that any prisoner can do.
studies.practice: Run the exact sequence today when anxiety spikes: name one reason to rejoice, pray it with thanks, then deliberately choose one true and lovely thing to think on.
questions: Paul writes this from prison. What does that do to the excuse "I'll rejoice when things improve"?
Why does God promise peace rather than promising to fix the circumstance?

quiz.prompt: What should replace anxiety, according to Paul?
choices: Waiting silently for feelings to change
quiz.explanation: Philippians 4:6: be careful for nothing; instead, pray with thanksgiving.

quiz.prompt: What will the peace of God do?
choices: Keep (guard) your hearts and minds through Christ Jesus
quiz.explanation: Philippians 4:7: peace stands guard; explanations are not promised.

studies.title: In him all things hold together
studies.passage: Who is the image of the invisible God, the firstborn of every creature: for by him were all things created, that are in heaven, and that are in earth, visible and invisible, whether they be thrones, or dominions, or principalities, or powers: all things were created by him, and for him: and he is before all things, and by him all things consist. And he is the head of the body, the church: who is the beginning, the firstborn from the dead; that in all things he might have the preeminence. For it pleased the Father that in him should all fulness dwell; and, having made peace through the blood of his cross, by him to reconcile all things unto himself; by him, I say, whether they be things in earth, or things in heaven.
studies.context: Paul sings of Christ as the image of the invisible God, creator of all things visible and invisible, before all things, holding all things together, head of the Church, firstborn from the dead, reconciling all things by the blood of his cross.
studies.orthodox: The Church set this hymn against every heresy that makes Christ a lesser being: if all things were made through him, he cannot himself be a made thing. "In him all things consist" is confessed of Jesus of Nazareth, crucified under Pontius Pilate.
studies.practice: When life feels like it is flying apart, pray the creed hidden in this passage: "Lord, you hold all things together — including this."
questions: If Christ made "thrones and dominions," what room is left for calling him a created being?
Paul moves from creation to cross in five verses. Why does the same Person have to do both?

quiz.prompt: Christ is called the image of...
choices: The visible God of Israel only
quiz.explanation: Colossians 1:15: the invisible God made visible — that is the incarnation.

quiz.prompt: By what does he reconcile all things?
choices: By the blood of his cross
quiz.explanation: Colossians 1:20: peace is made through the blood of his cross.

studies.title: He emptied himself
studies.passage: Let this mind be in you, which was also in Christ Jesus: who, being in the form of God, thought it not robbery to be equal with God: but made himself of no reputation, and took upon him the form of a servant, and was made in the likeness of men: and being found in fashion as a man, he humbled himself, and became obedient unto death, even the death of the cross. Wherefore God also hath highly exalted him, and given him a name which is above every name: that at the name of Jesus every knee should bow, of things in heaven, and things in earth, and things under the earth; and that every tongue should confess that Jesus Christ is Lord, to the glory of God the Father.
studies.context: Paul quotes what may be the Church's earliest hymn: Christ, being in the form of God, did not grasp at equality, emptied himself, took a servant's form, became obedient to death — even the death of the cross. Therefore God exalted him, and every knee shall bow.
studies.orthodox: The Fathers call this the kenosis: the Son does not stop being God; he adds our humility to his glory (St. Cyril). The hymn is given not as trivia but as a mind to copy: "Let this mind be in you."
studies.practice: Take the lowest task available to you today — the one nobody thanks — and do it as the mind of Christ, not as defeat.
questions: The hymn says he "thought it not robbery to be equal with God." What does refusing to grasp look like in an argument at home?
Why does the exaltation pass through the cross instead of around it?

quiz.prompt: What form did Christ take in his humbling?
choices: Only the appearance of a man
quiz.explanation: Philippians 2:7: a true servant's form — real humanity, really lowly.

quiz.prompt: What name is given him in exaltation?
choices: A name known only in heaven
The name above every name, at which every knee bows
The name of the highest angel
quiz.explanation: Philippians 2:9–10: exaltation answers humiliation.

studies.title: God has spoken by his Son
studies.passage: God, who at sundry times and in divers manners spake in time past unto the fathers by the prophets, hath in these last days spoken unto us by his Son, whom he hath appointed heir of all things, by whom also he made the worlds; who being the brightness of his glory, and the express image of his person, and upholding all things by the word of his power, when he had by himself purged our sins, sat down on the right hand of the Majesty on high; being made so much better than the angels, as he hath by inheritance obtained a more excellent name than they.
studies.context: God spoke of old in fragments through the prophets; now, in these last days, he has spoken in a Son — heir of all things, maker of the worlds, the brightness of his glory and exact image of his person, upholding all things by the word of his power.
studies.orthodox: The Church confesses the phrase without flinching: the Son is not God's best creature but the Father's own radiance, as light is from light. Hebrews will spend thirteen chapters proving the Son greater than angels, Moses, and priests — because only God can save.
studies.practice: Read the passage aloud and list everything said about the Son. Which one do you most need to believe today?
questions: Prophets spoke "in many parts and ways"; the Son is the whole speech. What changes when God's final word is a Person?
"Upholding all things by the word of his power" — what is Christ doing right now, between his ascension and return?

quiz.prompt: How did God speak in former times?
choices: Through the prophets, in many parts and manners
quiz.explanation: Hebrews 1:1: fragmentary then, complete in the Son now.

quiz.prompt: The Son is described as...
choices: The brightness of God's glory and the express image of his person
A prophet greater than Moses only
quiz.explanation: Hebrews 1:3: radiance and exact image — language of true divinity.

studies.title: The glory on the mountain
studies.passage: And after six days Jesus taketh Peter, James, and John his brother, and bringeth them up into an high mountain apart, and was transfigured before them: and his face did shine as the sun, and his raiment was white as the light. And, behold, there appeared unto them Moses and Elias talking with him. Then answered Peter, and said unto Jesus, Lord, it is good for us to be here: if thou wilt, let us make here three tabernacles; one for thee, and one for Moses, and one for Elias. While he yet spake, behold, a bright cloud overshadowed them: and behold a voice out of the cloud, which said, This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased; hear ye him. And when the disciples heard it, they fell on their face, and were sore afraid. And Jesus came and touched them, and said, Arise, and be not afraid. And when they had lifted up their eyes, they saw no man, save Jesus only.
studies.context: Jesus takes Peter, James, and John up a high mountain and is transfigured: his face shines like the sun, his garments become white as light. Moses and Elijah appear; the Father's voice names him beloved Son; the disciples fall on their faces in awe.
studies.orthodox: The Church keeps a whole feast for this (August 6) and sings that the light is uncreated — the very glory of God shown in a human body (St. Gregory Palamas). Christ does not become something new on Tabor; the disciples' eyes are opened to what he always is.
studies.practice: Sit somewhere bright today — sun on your face — and pray: "Lord, open my eyes to your glory in ordinary things."
questions: Why Moses and Elijah — what do the Law and the Prophets do standing beside Christ?
Jesus tells them to tell no one "until the Son of man is risen." Why the delay?

quiz.prompt: What happens to Jesus on the mountain?
choices: He receives glory from the Father for the first time
He is transfigured — face shining, garments white as light
He is carried up into heaven briefly
quiz.explanation: Matthew 17:2: transfigured before them; the glory is revealed, not newly given.

quiz.prompt: What does the Father's voice command?
choices: "This is my beloved Son... hear ye him"
quiz.explanation: Matthew 17:5: the voice repeats the baptism and adds the command — hear him.

studies.title: It is written
studies.passage: Then was Jesus led up of the Spirit into the wilderness to be tempted of the devil. And when he had fasted forty days and forty nights, he was afterward an hungred. And when the tempter came to him, he said, If thou be the Son of God, command that these stones be made bread. But he answered and said, It is written, Man shall not live by bread alone, but by every word that proceedeth out of the mouth of God. Then the devil taketh him up into the holy city, and setteth him on a pinnacle of the temple, and saith unto him, If thou be the Son of God, cast thyself down: for it is written, He shall give his angels charge concerning thee: And in their hands they shall bear thee up, Lest at any time thou dash thy foot against a stone. Jesus said unto him, It is written again, Thou shalt not tempt the Lord thy God. Again, the devil taketh him up into an exceeding high mountain, and sheweth him all the kingdoms of the world, and the glory of them; and saith unto him, All these things will I give thee, if thou wilt fall down and worship me. Then saith Jesus unto him, Get thee hence, Satan: for it is written, Thou shalt worship the Lord thy God, and him only shalt thou serve. Then the devil leaveth him, and, behold, angels came and ministered unto him.
studies.context: Fresh from baptism, the Spirit drives Jesus into the wilderness for forty days. The tempter offers bread without obedience, spectacle without trust, and kingdoms without the cross. Three times Jesus answers with Scripture — and only Scripture.
studies.orthodox: The Fathers see Adam reversed: where Adam fell with a full stomach in a garden, Christ stands hungry in a desert (St. Gregory the Great). He fights as a man, with the weapons given to men — fasting and the word — so his victory can be ours.
studies.practice: Face one temptation today the way he did: answer it out loud with a Scripture you know, and do not negotiate.
questions: Why does the Spirit himself lead Jesus into the place of testing?
Each temptation is a shortcut around the cross. What shortcut is being offered to you right now?

quiz.prompt: With what does Jesus answer every temptation?
choices: "It is written" — the word of God
quiz.explanation: Matthew 4:4, 7, 10: the sword of the Spirit is quoted Scripture.

quiz.prompt: How long does the fasting and testing last?
quiz.explanation: Matthew 4:2: forty days — recapitulating Israel's forty years, and succeeding.

studies.title: Good tidings of great joy
studies.passage: And there were in the same country shepherds abiding in the field, keeping watch over their flock by night. And, lo, the angel of the Lord came upon them, and the glory of the Lord shone round about them: and they were sore afraid. And the angel said unto them, Fear not: for, behold, I bring you good tidings of great joy, which shall be to all people. For unto you is born this day in the city of David a Saviour, which is Christ the Lord. And this shall be a sign unto you; Ye shall find the babe wrapped in swaddling clothes, lying in a manger. And suddenly there was with the angel a multitude of the heavenly host praising God, and saying, Glory to God in the highest, And on earth peace, good will toward men. And it came to pass, as the angels were gone away from them into heaven, the shepherds said one to another, Let us now go even unto Bethlehem, and see this thing which is come to pass, which the Lord hath made known unto us. And they came with haste, and found Mary, and Joseph, and the babe lying in a manger. And when they had seen it, they made known abroad the saying which was told them concerning this child. And all they that heard it wondered at those things which were told them by the shepherds. But Mary kept all these things, and pondered them in her heart. And the shepherds returned, glorifying and praising God for all the things that they had heard and seen, as it was told unto them.
studies.context: The birth of the world's king is announced not to the palace but to shepherds in night fields: "Fear not... unto you is born this day in the city of David a Saviour, which is Christ the Lord." A multitude of heaven's army sings; shepherds run, see, and tell.
studies.orthodox: The Church marvels at the audience: the first evangelists of the incarnation are shepherds — the overlooked. The sign given is not power but a baby in a feeding trough: God's glory arrives small, poor, and holdable.
studies.practice: Tell one person today, simply, why Christ's birth is good news — the way the shepherds did: what you heard, what you saw.
questions: Why shepherds? What does the choice of audience say about God's kingdom before a word is preached?
"Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace" — how can peace begin with a baby in a trough?

quiz.prompt: Where is the Saviour announced to be born?
choices: In Bethlehem, the city of David
quiz.explanation: Luke 2:11: Bethlehem, as Micah foretold.

quiz.prompt: What is the sign given to the shepherds?
choices: A babe wrapped in swaddling clothes, lying in a manger
quiz.explanation: Luke 2:12: the sign of God's arrival is humility.

studies.title: We have seen his star
studies.passage: Now when Jesus was born in Bethlehem of Judæa in the days of Herod the king, behold, there came wise men from the east to Jerusalem, saying, Where is he that is born King of the Jews? for we have seen his star in the east, and are come to worship him. When Herod the king had heard these things, he was troubled, and all Jerusalem with him. And when he had gathered all the chief priests and scribes of the people together, he demanded of them where Christ should be born. And they said unto him, In Bethlehem of Judæa: for thus it is written by the prophet, And thou Bethlehem, in the land of Juda, Art not the least among the princes of Juda: For out of thee shall come a Governor, That shall rule my people Israel. Then Herod, when he had privily called the wise men, enquired of them diligently what time the star appeared. And he sent them to Bethlehem, and said, Go and search diligently for the young child; and when ye have found him, bring me word again, that I may come and worship him also. When they had heard the king, they departed; and, lo, the star, which they saw in the east, went before them, till it came and stood over where the young child was. When they saw the star, they rejoiced with exceeding great joy. And when they were come into the house, they saw the young child with Mary his mother, and fell down, and worshipped him: and when they had opened their treasures, they presented unto him gifts; gold, and frankincense, and myrrh. And being warned of God in a dream that they should not return to Herod, they departed into their own country another way.
studies.context: Wise men from the east follow a star to Jerusalem, unsettle a king, and find the child in a house in Bethlehem. Falling down, they worship, and open treasures: gold, frankincense, and myrrh. Warned in a dream, they go home another way.
studies.orthodox: The Church reads the gifts as prophecy in objects: gold for a king, frankincense for God, myrrh for the burial of the one who would die (St. Irenaeus). Gentile astrologers are the first worshippers — and Herod, with all his Scripture scholars, only plots.
studies.practice: Like the magi, bring Christ one real gift this week — time, money, or a forgiven debt — and be willing to go home "another way" if he redirects you.
questions: Herod's scholars know exactly where the Messiah is born (Micah 5:2) and never go. What does knowledge without worship become?
Why does Matthew bother telling us the gifts? What does each one say?

quiz.prompt: What do the wise men do when they find the child?
choices: They report back to Herod at once
They fall down and worship him, offering gifts
They ask Mary to prove his identity
quiz.explanation: Matthew 2:11: Gentiles worship before Israel's king hears of it.

quiz.prompt: Why do they not return to Herod?
choices: The road was blocked by soldiers
Warned by God in a dream
They lost their way in the desert
quiz.explanation: Matthew 2:12: warned in a dream, they depart another way — obedience over reporting.

studies.title: Holy, holy, holy
studies.passage: In the year that king Uzziah died I saw also the Lord sitting upon a throne, high and lifted up, and his train filled the temple. Above it stood the seraphims: each one had six wings; with twain he covered his face, and with twain he covered his feet, and with twain he did fly. And one cried unto another, and said, Holy, holy, holy, is the LORD of hosts: the whole earth is full of his glory. And the posts of the door moved at the voice of him that cried, and the house was filled with smoke. Then said I, Woe is me! for I am undone; because I am a man of unclean lips, and I dwell in the midst of a people of unclean lips: for mine eyes have seen the King, the LORD of hosts. Then flew one of the seraphims unto me, having a live coal in his hand, which he had taken with the tongs from off the altar: and he laid it upon my mouth, and said, Lo, this hath touched thy lips; and thine iniquity is taken away, and thy sin purged. Also I heard the voice of the Lord, saying, Whom shall I send, and who will go for us? Then said I, Here am I; send me.
studies.context: In the year King Uzziah dies, Isaiah sees the King who cannot die: enthroned, robed, the temple shaking, seraphim crying "Holy, holy, holy." Isaiah cries "Woe is me," a coal touches his lips, and the call comes: "Whom shall I send?" — "Here am I; send me."
studies.orthodox: The Church sings the seraphim's hymn at every liturgy ("Holy, holy, holy" in the anaphora) and reads the vision as a glimpse of the Trinity — one Lord, thrice holy (St. Basil). Isaiah is not qualified by talent but by cleansing: the coal comes before the commission.
studies.practice: Before asking God for a task, ask for the coal: confess one specific uncleanness today and receive his cleansing, then say "send me."
questions: Isaiah's first word on seeing God is "Woe is me," not "How beautiful." Why is conviction the doorway, not the obstacle?
The coal cleanses before the call. Where do we try to reverse that order?

quiz.prompt: What do the seraphim cry?
choices: "Holy, holy, holy, is the Lord of hosts"
quiz.explanation: Isaiah 6:3: the thrice-holy hymn the Church still sings.

quiz.prompt: What touches Isaiah's lips?
choices: A live coal from the altar
quiz.explanation: Isaiah 6:6–7: the altar's coal takes away his iniquity.

studies.title: Can these bones live?
studies.passage: The hand of the LORD was upon me, and carried me out in the spirit of the LORD, and set me down in the midst of the valley which was full of bones, and caused me to pass by them round about: and, behold, there were very many in the open valley; and, lo, they were very dry. And he said unto me, Son of man, can these bones live? And I answered, O Lord GOD, thou knowest. Again he said unto me, Prophesy upon these bones, and say unto them, O ye dry bones, hear the word of the LORD. Thus saith the Lord GOD unto these bones; Behold, I will cause breath to enter into you, and ye shall live: and I will lay sinews upon you, and will bring up flesh upon you, and cover you with skin, and put breath in you, and ye shall live; and ye shall know that I am the LORD. So I prophesied as I was commanded: and as I prophesied, there was a noise, and behold a shaking, and the bones came together, bone to his bone. And when I beheld, lo, the sinews and the flesh came up upon them, and the skin covered them above: but there was no breath in them. Then said he unto me, Prophesy unto the wind, prophesy, son of man, and say to the wind, Thus saith the Lord GOD; Come from the four winds, O breath, and breathe upon these slain, that they may live. So I prophesied as he commanded me, and the breath came into them, and they lived, and stood up upon their feet, an exceeding great army.
studies.context: Ezekiel is set in a valley of very dry bones — a dead nation. At God's word he prophesies; bones rattle together, flesh comes, and at the breath (ruach) the slain stand up, "an exceeding great army."
studies.orthodox: The Church reads this at gravesides and in Holy Week: resurrection is not resuscitation of the strong but God's breath in the utterly dead. The bones are "very many" and "very dry" — the honesty comes before the hope.
studies.practice: Name the driest area of your life to God today using his own question: "Can these bones live?" Then answer as Ezekiel did: "O Lord God, thou knowest."
questions: Why does God ask Ezekiel "Can these bones live?" instead of simply performing the miracle?
The bones come together first, but life waits for the breath. What in your life is assembled but not yet alive?

quiz.prompt: What does Ezekiel answer when asked if the bones can live?
quiz.explanation: Ezekiel 37:3: faith without presumption — God knows.

quiz.prompt: What finally makes the bodies live?
quiz.explanation: Ezekiel 37:9–10: prophesy to the breath — God's Spirit is the life.

studies.title: What does the Lord require?
studies.passage: Wherewith shall I come before the LORD, and bow myself before the high God? shall I come before him with burnt offerings, with calves of a year old? Will the LORD be pleased with thousands of rams, or with ten thousands of rivers of oil? shall I give my firstborn for my transgression, the fruit of my body for the sin of my soul? He hath shewed thee, O man, what is good; and what doth the LORD require of thee, but to do justly, and to love mercy, and to walk humbly with thy God?
studies.context: Israel asks what to bring God: thousands of rams? rivers of oil? a firstborn? The prophet cuts through the bargaining: "He hath shewed thee, O man, what is good" — do justly, love mercy, walk humbly with thy God.
studies.orthodox: The Church reads Micah against every attempt to buy God: sacrifice matters, but the sacrifice God wants is a just, merciful, humble life (cf. Hosea 6:6). The three verbs are a whole rule of life in one breath.
studies.practice: Do one just act, one merciful act, and one humble act today. Small counts; hidden counts more.
questions: Why does God refuse the escalating offers (rams, oil, firstborn)? What is he protecting us from believing about him?
Which of the three — justice, mercy, humility — is your weakest, and what would it look like this week?

quiz.prompt: What does God require, in Micah's summary?
choices: Do justly, love mercy, walk humbly with thy God
quiz.explanation: Micah 6:8: three verbs that cannot be outsourced to a temple.

quiz.prompt: How does the passage say God has already made this known?
choices: "He hath shewed thee, O man, what is good"
Through a new vision given to Micah alone
In a dream to the king
quiz.explanation: Micah 6:8: the requirement is not a secret; it has been shown.

studies.title: Yet I will rejoice
studies.passage: Although the fig tree shall not blossom, Neither shall fruit be in the vines; The labour of the olive shall fail, And the fields shall yield no meat; The flock shall be cut off from the fold, And there shall be no herd in the stalls: Yet I will rejoice in the LORD, I will joy in the God of my salvation. The LORD God is my strength, And he will make my feet like hinds' feet, And he will make me to walk upon mine high places. To the chief singer on my stringed instruments.
studies.context: Habakkuk lists total loss — no figs, no grapes, no cattle, empty fields — and then writes the Bible's defiant "yet": "Yet I will rejoice in the Lord, I will joy in the God of my salvation." God becomes his strength, giving him deer's feet on high places.
studies.orthodox: The Church prays Habakkuk in the morning canon of hymns: joy here is not denial; every loss is named before the "yet." Faith is not pretending the fields are full — it is locating joy in God when they are empty.
studies.practice: Write your own "yet" today: name your losses honestly on paper, then finish the sentence — "Yet I will rejoice in the Lord, because..."
questions: Why does Habakkuk name every loss before rejoicing instead of skipping to praise?
Where is his joy located — in circumstances restored, or somewhere else?

quiz.prompt: When does Habakkuk rejoice?
choices: While the fields are still empty
quiz.explanation: Habakkuk 3:17–18: the "yet" comes before any change in circumstance.

quiz.prompt: What does God make of Habakkuk's feet?
choices: Feet like deer's feet, set on high places
Feet swift to escape the land
quiz.explanation: Habakkuk 3:19: strength to stand on heights, not escape from the valley.

studies.title: I know that my Redeemer lives
studies.passage: Oh that my words were now written! Oh that they were printed in a book! That they were graven with an iron pen and lead In the rock for ever! For I know that my redeemer liveth, And that he shall stand at the latter day upon the earth: And though after my skin worms destroy this body, Yet in my flesh shall I see God: Whom I shall see for myself, And mine eyes shall behold, and not another; Though my reins be consumed within me. … Then Job answered the LORD, and said, I know that thou canst do every thing, And that no thought can be withholden from thee. Who is he that hideth counsel without knowledge? Therefore have I uttered that I understood not; Things too wonderful for me, which I knew not. Hear, I beseech thee, and I will speak: I will demand of thee, and declare thou unto me. I have heard of thee by the hearing of the ear: But now mine eye seeth thee. Wherefore I abhor myself, and repent In dust and ashes.
studies.context: Everything taken, friends accusing, Job refuses to curse God or confess sins he did not commit. From the ash heap he cries the Old Testament's resurrection hope: "I know that my redeemer liveth... in my flesh shall I see God." At the end he sees, and repents in dust and ashes.
studies.orthodox: The Church reads Job in Holy Week beside Christ's suffering: the righteous sufferer who will not let go of God. Job's friends speak true sentences wrongly — the book warns us how not to comfort — while Job's honesty ("though he slay me, yet will I trust in him") is vindicated.
studies.practice: In prayer today, say the hard thing to God exactly as it is — no editing. Then sit in silence two minutes, the way Job sat seven days.
questions: Job's friends explain his suffering; Job questions God to his face. Which does God vindicate at the end?
"In my flesh shall I see God" — why does the flesh matter to the hope?

quiz.prompt: What does Job declare from the ash heap?
quiz.explanation: Job 19:25: resurrection hope centuries before the resurrection.

quiz.prompt: How does Job end after seeing God?
choices: Repenting in dust and ashes, humbled and comforted
Cursing the day of his birth again
quiz.explanation: Job 42:5–6: "Mine eye seeth thee" — sight replaces hearsay.

studies.title: The fear of the Lord
studies.passage: My son, forget not my law; But let thine heart keep my commandments: For length of days, and long life, And peace, shall they add to thee. Let not mercy and truth forsake thee: Bind them about thy neck; Write them upon the table of thine heart: So shalt thou find favour and good understanding In the sight of God and man. Trust in the LORD with all thine heart; And lean not unto thine own understanding. In all thy ways acknowledge him, And he shall direct thy paths. Be not wise in thine own eyes: Fear the LORD, and depart from evil. It shall be health to thy navel, And marrow to thy bones. Honour the LORD with thy substance, And with the firstfruits of all thine increase: So shall thy barns be filled with plenty, And thy presses shall burst out with new wine. My son, despise not the chastening of the LORD; Neither be weary of his correction: For whom the LORD loveth he correcteth; Even as a father the son in whom he delighteth.
studies.context: A father teaches his son: trust in the Lord with all your heart, lean not on your own understanding, honor the Lord with your firstfruits, and do not despise his correction — he corrects those he loves.
studies.orthodox: The Church reads Proverbs as Christ the Wisdom of God teaching household life (1 Corinthians 1:30). Its promise-shape is true in the long run without being a vending machine: trust is a direction, not a transaction.
studies.practice: Honor the Lord with firstfruits this week: give before you spend, not from what is left over. Trust him with one decision you keep leaning on your own understanding for.
questions: "Lean not unto thine own understanding" — what is the difference between using your mind and leaning on it?
Why does correction prove love here instead of rejection?

quiz.prompt: What are we told to trust with all the heart?
quiz.explanation: Proverbs 3:5: whole-heart trust, not self-leaning.

quiz.prompt: How does God correct those he loves, in this picture?
choices: As a father corrects the son he delights in
As a judge condemns a criminal
quiz.explanation: Proverbs 3:12: fatherly correction — delight, not disgust.

studies.title: Vanity of vanities — and the conclusion
studies.passage: Remember now thy Creator in the days of thy youth, while the evil days come not, nor the years draw nigh, when thou shalt say, I have no pleasure in them; … or ever the silver cord be loosed, or the golden bowl be broken, or the pitcher be broken at the fountain, or the wheel broken at the cistern. Then shall the dust return to the earth as it was: and the spirit shall return unto God who gave it. Vanity of vanities, saith the Preacher; all is vanity. … Let us hear the conclusion of the whole matter: Fear God, and keep his commandments: for this is the whole duty of man. For God shall bring every work into judgment, with every secret thing, whether it be good, or whether it be evil.
studies.context: The Preacher has tested pleasure, wealth, work, and wisdom, and found them all vapor. The book closes: remember your Creator in your youth, and — the whole matter concluded — fear God and keep his commandments, for God will judge every work.
studies.orthodox: The Church keeps Ecclesiastes in the Bible as holy realism: a rich king's lab report on life "under the sun." Its honesty about emptiness is the doorway; its conclusion points beyond the sun, where judgment and remembrance matter.
studies.practice: Remember your Creator with one concrete act today — before the day's vapor settles: pray first, give first, forgive first.
questions: Why does a book of the Bible spend twelve chapters calling everything vanity — what is it saving us from?
"Remember thy Creator in the days of thy youth" — why youth, specifically?

quiz.prompt: What is "the conclusion of the whole matter"?
choices: Fear God and keep his commandments
Wealth is the final proof of blessing
quiz.explanation: Ecclesiastes 12:13: after all the vapor, one firm floor.

quiz.prompt: What will God do with every work?
choices: Bring every work into judgment, including every secret thing
quiz.explanation: Ecclesiastes 12:14: nothing is vapor to the Judge.

studies.title: Faith without works is dead
studies.passage: What doth it profit, my brethren, though a man say he hath faith, and have not works? can faith save him? If a brother or sister be naked, and destitute of daily food, and one of you say unto them, Depart in peace, be ye warmed and filled; notwithstanding ye give them not those things which are needful to the body; what doth it profit? Even so faith, if it hath not works, is dead, being alone. Yea, a man may say, Thou hast faith, and I have works: shew me thy faith without thy works, and I will shew thee my faith by my works. Thou believest that there is one God; thou doest well: the devils also believe, and tremble. But wilt thou know, O vain man, that faith without works is dead? Was not Abraham our father justified by works, when he had offered Isaac his son upon the altar? Seest thou how faith wrought with his works, and by works was faith made perfect? And the scripture was fulfilled which saith, Abraham believed God, and it was imputed unto him for righteousness: and he was called the Friend of God. Ye see then how that by works a man is justified, and not by faith only. Likewise also was not Rahab the harlot justified by works, when she had received the messengers, and had sent them out another way? For as the body without the spirit is dead, so faith without works is dead also.
studies.context: James presses a hard question: can a faith that only talks save? A brother sent away with kind words and no coat has received nothing. Abraham's faith was completed by works; Rahab's likewise. "Faith without works is dead."
studies.orthodox: The Church reads Paul and James as friends, not opponents: Paul attacks law-keeping as a rival system of earning; James attacks dead profession that never moves a hand. Living faith works through love (Galatians 5:6) — fruit, not root-wages.
studies.practice: Find one "be warm and filled" moment today and replace the words with the actual coat, meal, ride, or visit.
questions: James uses Abraham; Paul uses Abraham (Romans 4). How can both be right?
What is the difference between works added to faith and faith that works?

quiz.prompt: What does James call faith without works?
quiz.explanation: James 2:17, 26: alone and unworking, faith is dead.

quiz.prompt: Whose faith does James say was "made perfect" by works?
quiz.explanation: James 2:22: Abraham's faith was completed — perfected — by his works.

studies.title: A living hope through the resurrection
studies.passage: Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, which according to his abundant mercy hath begotten us again unto a lively hope by the resurrection of Jesus Christ from the dead, to an inheritance incorruptible, and undefiled, and that fadeth not away, reserved in heaven for you, who are kept by the power of God through faith unto salvation ready to be revealed in the last time. Wherein ye greatly rejoice, though now for a season, if need be, ye are in heaviness through manifold temptations: that the trial of your faith, being much more precious than of gold that perisheth, though it be tried with fire, might be found unto praise and honour and glory at the appearing of Jesus Christ: whom having not seen, ye love; in whom, though now ye see him not, yet believing, ye rejoice with joy unspeakable and full of glory: receiving the end of your faith, even the salvation of your souls. … Beloved, think it not strange concerning the fiery trial which is to try you, as though some strange thing happened unto you: but rejoice, inasmuch as ye are partakers of Christ's sufferings; that, when his glory shall be revealed, ye may be glad also with exceeding joy.
studies.context: To scattered, suffering believers Peter writes of a living hope by the resurrection, an inheritance incorruptible kept in heaven, and trials that test faith like fire tests gold — precious, and temporary. "Beloved, think it not strange concerning the fiery trial."
studies.orthodox: St. Peter writes as one who himself would be crucified: the hope is "living" because Christ is alive, not because circumstances improve. The Church reads 1 Peter at baptisms — the trials do not mean God lost your address; the inheritance is being kept.
studies.practice: Thank God today for the inheritance "kept in heaven" while one thing on earth feels unkept. Name both, honestly.
questions: Why does tested faith come out more precious than gold, which also is tested by fire?
Peter says rejoice in the trial (4:13). What makes that possible without pretending?

quiz.prompt: What kind of hope does Peter announce?
choices: A hope that trials never come
A living hope by the resurrection of Jesus Christ
quiz.explanation: 1 Peter 1:3: living, because the One who rose is alive.

quiz.prompt: How should believers view the fiery trial?
choices: As proof God has left them
Not strange — rejoice, as partakers of Christ's sufferings
As a sign to hide their faith
quiz.explanation: 1 Peter 4:12–13: fiery, shared with Christ, and temporary.

studies.title: God is love
studies.passage: Beloved, let us love one another: for love is of God; and every one that loveth is born of God, and knoweth God. He that loveth not knoweth not God; for God is love. In this was manifested the love of God toward us, because that God sent his only begotten Son into the world, that we might live through him. Herein is love, not that we loved God, but that he loved us, and sent his Son to be the propitiation for our sins. Beloved, if God so loved us, we ought also to love one another. No man hath seen God at any time. If we love one another, God dwelleth in us, and his love is perfected in us. … There is no fear in love; but perfect love casteth out fear: because fear hath torment. He that feareth is not made perfect in love. We love him, because he first loved us.
studies.context: The aged apostle circles one truth: God is love; love is defined at the cross ("not that we loved God, but that he loved us"); and love that refuses to love the brother is not God's love at all. Perfect love casts out fear.
studies.orthodox: The Church reads 1 John as the examination of conscience for every claim to know God: theology that does not become love of the visible brother is exposed as noise. "We love him, because he first loved us" — the order is everything.
studies.practice: Do the passage: pick the brother or sister hardest to love and do one deliberate act of love before you ask God for more feeling.
questions: John defines love by what God did, not by what we feel. How does that steady love on bad days?
"No man hath seen God... if we love one another, God dwelleth in us" — where does John say God becomes visible?

quiz.prompt: How is God's love shown, per John?
choices: In that he sent his Son to be the propitiation for our sins
In giving us whatever we ask
quiz.explanation: 1 John 4:10: love is defined at the sending of the Son.

quiz.prompt: What does perfect love cast out?
quiz.explanation: 1 John 4:18: perfect love casteth out fear — punishment's dread does not survive love.

studies.title: Behold, I make all things new
studies.passage: And I saw a new heaven and a new earth: for the first heaven and the first earth were passed away; and there was no more sea. And I John saw the holy city, new Jerusalem, coming down from God out of heaven, prepared as a bride adorned for her husband. And I heard a great voice out of heaven saying, Behold, the tabernacle of God is with men, and he will dwell with them, and they shall be his people, and God himself shall be with them, and be their God. And God shall wipe away all tears from their eyes; and there shall be no more death, neither sorrow, nor crying, neither shall there be any more pain: for the former things are passed away.
